findings.issue_text: [BUG] The user-storage isValid() for recovery codes accepts any code from the stored list via generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())) and never consumes or invalidates the used code. Any code that was already used (or an out-of-sequence code) keeps authenticating forever through the credentialManager().isValid path, diverging from the one-time sequential semantics of the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider that the storage path is supposed to mirror; the test fixture therefore certifies replayable recovery codes as valid federated behavior.

[ADVISORY] The diff substantially modifies BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage, a fixture whose own javadoc states it was created in Keycloak 4.8.3 so that 'Future Keycloak versions should work fine without a need to change the code of this provider'. The backwards-compatibility guarantee this provider exists to verify (that an unmodified 4.8.3-era storage provider keeps working against current Keycloak) is silently weakened: the suite now tests a provider that was co-evolved with the new feature, so a regression that only manifests with genuinely old providers would no longer be caught. A dedicated new test storage provider would have preserved that invariant.

[ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential hard-codes the provider id string "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" in session.getProvider(CredentialProvider.class, "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes") instead of using RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID, whose import was even removed from RecoveryAuthnCodesAction in this same diff. The provider id is now maintained in two places (the factory constant and this literal); a rename or a custom CredentialProvider registered under a different id in a realm leaves createRecoveryCodesCredential silently resolving null and falling into the local createCredential branch, storing recovery codes in the wrong place for federated users with no error.

[ADVISORY] testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin performs exactly one recovery-code login and never re-authenticates to assert that the used code was consumed (code #1 requested next, or code #0 rejected). A regression in the consume path for federated credentials — e.g. the post-validation credential update not being routed to the user storage, leaving all codes valid indefinitely — passes this test silently; the suite would certify replayable recovery codes for federated users as working.

[ADVISORY] getCredential checks the federated storage first and only falls back to locally stored credentials, establishing a priority order between two possible copies of the same credential type without any invariant that only one copy exists. If a federated user ever holds both a stale local copy (e.g. created by an older version or out-of-band admin operation) and a storage copy, login validation and code consumption operate on the federated copy while any consumer that still reads getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream directly (outside this diff) sees the stale local one, and the two copies can diverge with no cleanup path.

[ADVISORY] The constructor wraps the lookup in Optional via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) but immediately calls credentialModelOpt.get() unguarded, so the Optional conveys safety that is not actually delivered. A user without recovery codes in either store who reaches the recovery-codes form rendering gets a NoSuchElementException/500 instead of a graceful skip; the new Optional-based lookup broadens the paths that reach this .get() without adding the handling its shape implies.

[ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential takes both credentialModel and generatedCodes — two parallel representations of the same data — and the storage branch re-serializes generatedCodes with JsonSerialization while the local branch persists credentialModel as-is. The serialized payload written to user storage (JSON of the raw list) and the payload stored locally (credentialModel.getCredentialData()) are produced at two independent sites; if credentialModel construction ever changes shape (adds metadata or a wrapper object), federated and local users silently end up with differently-shaped credentialData, and storage providers deserializing with readValue(..., List.class) break at login time.

[BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential persists the raw, unhashed generatedCodes list as a plaintext JSON array in the user-storage branch (UserCredentialModel challengeResponse -> setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())), while the local branch persists the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel built via createFromValues, which stores hashed codes. For any user backed by a storage provider that supports the recovery-codes type, the backup codes shown to the end user are persisted verbatim (unhashed) in the external store, whereas the identical credential created for a non-federated user is stored hashed in the Keycloak DB; a read of the external store yields usable recovery codes, and the BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid branch (key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())) confirms the plaintext-at-rest semantics this diff establishes.

[ADVISORY] The user-storage contract introduced here hands providers a bare JSON array of codes in UserCredentialModel.getChallengeResponse() rather than the canonical RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel payload that RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel expects when reading the credential back. Third-party user-storage providers that follow the established OTP precedent in this same class (store challengeResponse, return the stored CredentialModel verbatim from getCredentials) will hand the authenticator a credential whose credentialData is a plain array; createFromCredentialModel in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator/RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean then fails to parse it and the code-entry page breaks. The in-repo test provider only works because BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials silently re-wraps the raw list via createFromValues, a step the CredentialHelper API does not document or enforce.

[ADVISORY] The credential provider is looked up with the hardcoded string literal "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" while this same PR deletes the use of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID from RecoveryAuthnCodesAction, leaving the canonical constant unused at the new call site. If PROVIDER_ID is ever renamed, this call site silently returns null and createRecoveryCodesCredential throws an NPE instead of failing at compile time; the next change to the provider id now has to be hunted through string literals.

[ADVISORY] The storage provider's updateCredential blindly overwrites the stored recovery-codes credentialData with input.getChallengeResponse(), so whatever the authenticator sends when it rewrites the credential to consume the just-used code replaces the entire stored codes list. If the consume-update issued by RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator after a successful code entry carries anything other than the full remaining-codes JSON in challengeResponse, the stored credential is corrupted or wiped and every subsequent recovery-code login for that federated user fails; the new test performs exactly one recovery-code login, so a first-use code consumption bug of this shape passes CI unnoticed.

[ADVISORY] getCredential unconditionally prefers the federated credential over the locally stored one, so a federated user who already has a recovery-codes credential in the Keycloak DB (created before their storage provider gained support for the type) ends up with two credentials of the same type, and createRecoveryCodesCredential writes new setups into the storage while the stale local copy remains. After an upgrade where a storage provider starts claiming the recovery-codes type, existing users' locally stored codes are shadowed (never read, never updated, never consumed) while fresh setups fork state across two stores; used-code counters can desynchronize between the copies and the DB credential becomes an unremovable leftover from the user's perspective.

[ADVISORY] testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin covers only the single happy-path login: it never exercises a second recovery-code login, a wrong-code attempt, or the used-code consumption round-trip through the federated updateCredential path introduced by this diff. The core semantics that differentiate the storage-backed path from the local one (one-time-use enforcement and re-read of the rewritten credential) have zero coverage; a regression in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential or in the challengeResponse payload contract would ship undetected while the existing assertions stay green.

[ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw, unhashed recovery codes (recoveryCodesJson = JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)) and hands them to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(), while the local-storage fallback path stores the hashed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel — the federated path persists plaintext recovery codes by design of this helper. Any user-storage backend following this contract (as the diff's own BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does: recoveryCodesModel.setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse()) storing the raw JSON list) holds fully usable recovery codes in plaintext in the external store (LDAP attribute, external DB), where the same codes stored locally are hashed; an attacker with read access to the user-storage backend obtains working second-factor recovery material that the local path was designed to never expose. The asymmetry contradicts the protection the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider provides.

[BUG] The new recovery-codes branch of isValid() validates with generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())), which accepts any of the user's codes regardless of which code number the login flow requested and never consumes or invalidates a used code — deviating from the position-bound, one-time semantics of the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider this PR claims compatibility with. Because this provider is the reference implementation of the new user-storage recovery-codes SPI contract introduced by this PR, the demonstrated contract is 'set-membership check on plaintext codes with no position binding and no single-use enforcement': a code entered for position 7 is accepted when code 3 was requested, and a compromised or observed code remains valid forever. The compatibility test suite then validates and blesses weaker validation semantics than production recovery-code behavior.

[ADVISORY] getCredential() resolves the federated credential first and only falls back to the locally stored credential via .or(), so when a user has both, the federated copy silently shadows the local one for both rendering (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean) and validation (RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator). A user whose credential was previously written to local storage (hashed, position-bound, single-use) and who is later federated with a storage that claims support for the type gets the federated plaintext, replayable copy used for every validation; the better-protected local credential is unreachable through this lookup, and the write path in createRecoveryCodesCredential reinforces the same preference, leaving the stale local copy permanently orphaned.

[ADVISORY] The constructor calls credentialModelOpt.get() on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without an isPresent check, throwing NoSuchElementException when the user has no recovery-codes credential in either federated or local storage. If the recovery-codes authenticator renders the challenge for a user with no resolvable credential (e.g., storage reports the type as configured but getCredentials() returns an empty stream, or a storage error path leaves neither location populated), the freemarker render fails with NoSuchElementException and the user gets a server error page instead of a graceful authentication failure or redirect.

[ADVISORY] The new fallback branch in createRecoveryCodesCredential (updateCredential returning false -> recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential locally) is never exercised by the only test added in this diff, which exclusively covers the storage-hit path. The diff's test (testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin) uses BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage whose updateCredential always returns true for recovery codes, so the else-branch that persists locally is unverified by any test in this diff; a regression there (e.g., wrong credentialModel passed to createCredential) would only surface for non-federated users, outside this test. Checked test files in the diff: testsuite/integration-arquillian/tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/federation/storage/BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.java — it contains no case where updateCredential returns false.

[ADVISORY] The new .or() fallback in getCredential (federated stream empty -> look in getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream) is not triggered by the test added in this diff, because the federated storage always returns the credential first. If the lookup ordering or the or() supplier itself regresses (e.g., the wrong type filter in the stored-credentials stream), the diff's only new test still passes because it never reaches the fallback; a federated-less user's recovery-code lookup breakage would be invisible to this diff's verification. Checked BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.java — the user 'otp1' is federated with recovery codes present, so findFirst() always succeeds and or() is dead in the test.

[ADVISORY] The new recovery-codes branch of isValid() has three failure returns (storedRecoveryKeys == null, IOException on deserialization, no matching key) and the diff's test never submits an incorrect or missing credential, so none of these branches is exercised. The fixture's negative path is unverified: if the anyMatch comparison or the null/deserialization guards were wrong (e.g., accepting any input), testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin would still pass because it only enters the correct code from the page; the suite gives no signal that wrong codes are actually rejected for storage-backed users. Checked BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.java — enterRecoveryCodes only enters generatedRecoveryAuthnCodes.get(requestedCode), never a wrong value.

[ADVISORY] testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin verifies only a single successful use of recovery code 0 and contains no assertion that the used code is invalidated (re-login rejects it or the next login demands code 1), so non-single-use behavior of storage-backed recovery codes passes the suite undetected. The new BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid branch compares the input with generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(...) and never consumes the used code; if code consumption does not round-trip through the federated storage, a federated user can replay the same recovery code forever, and this test — the only one in the diff covering the storage-backed login — stays green because it stops after the first successful login and never logs in again.

[ADVISORY] getCredentials() swallows the IOException from deserializing the stored recovery codes and silently returns the stream without that credential, while the parallel isValid() path in the same class treats the same corruption as a failed validation, so the two read paths disagree on the same corrupted state. If the serialized credentialData format drifts (exactly the scenario a backwards-compatibility fixture exists to catch), getCredentials silently drops the credential — getCredential() in RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils then finds nothing and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean's credentialModelOpt.get() throws NoSuchElementException — and the log.error (which omits the exception itself) is the only trace, making fixture failures hard to diagnose; the divergence from isValid's return-false handling means a corrupted credential is 'absent' for listing but 'invalid' for login.

[ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential switches the write path to user-storage-first without any cleanup or migration of a pre-existing locally-stored recovery-codes credential, so re-running the setup action for a federated user creates a second copy of the codes in the user storage while the old DB copy stays behind. For a federated user who already has recovery codes in the local DB (the only place the pre-change code wrote them — the old authenticator read getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream exclusively and it worked, proving old writes were local), re-running CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES after upgrade writes a new copy into the user storage; RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential reads federated-first, so the DB copy is permanently shadowed yet remains a live, valid credential set that no path in this diff ever removes — two divergent code sets in two stores, and the local one resurfaces if the storage-side copy is ever deleted.

[ADVISORY] The write path (user-storage-first here) and the read path (federated-first in RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential) both change in one release with no transition guard, creating a rolling-deploy skew where an old-version pod's authenticator still reads only getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream. In a mixed-version cluster, a user of a storage provider that supports the recovery-codes type sets up codes on a new-version pod (stored only in user storage); when the login attempt lands on an old-version pod, isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid finds no stored credential and rejects the user with INVALID_CREDENTIALS until every pod is upgraded. Today only the testsuite BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage declares support, so production impact is nil until third-party providers adopt the type, but the pattern has no expand/contract transition.

[ADVISORY] getCredentials silently drops the recovery-codes credential on a JSON deserialization failure (log.error only, model not added), so the credential disappears from the federated stream without any error surfaced to the caller. When credentialData cannot be parsed, getCredential falls through to the local store (also empty), RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean's credentialModelOpt.get() throws NoSuchElementException, and the user gets a 500-style error on the login page instead of a meaningful message — the data corruption is masked as a missing credential with only a server-side log line.

[BUG] RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean constructor calls credentialModelOpt.get() on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user), throwing NoSuchElementException (rendered as a raw 500) whenever no recovery-codes credential is found in either store. The new federated-first lookup introduces a reachable empty case the old code did not have: for a federated user whose storage reports the credential as configured (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isConfiguredFor returns true whenever myUser.recoveryCodes != null) but whose getCredentials drops the credential because JSON deserialization failed (the IOException catch at lines ~238-240 of the storage swallows it and returns the credential list without it), getCredential finds nothing in the federated stream and nothing locally, and the bean constructor throws NoSuchElementException mid-login-flow, producing a 500 error page instead of a graceful flow failure.

[ADVISORY] When user.credentialManager().updateCredential() returns false, the credential is silently re-created in the local Keycloak DB with no log line on the else branch — the only logged path is the successful user-storage write. Operators and admins auditing where recovery codes live get zero trace of the fallback: a deployment that expects codes persisted in the federated user store silently ends up with them only in the Keycloak DB, and debugging 'where did the codes go' after a storage-provider change has no log to start from.

[ADVISORY] The credential provider is looked up with the hardcoded string literal "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" while the diff removes the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID import, so a future rename of the provider id compiles cleanly but getProvider returns null. On the local-fallback path (updateCredential returning false), recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential would throw a NullPointerException during the required-action request, surfacing as a 500 at the exact moment a user is setting up their recovery codes; the removed constant was the compile-time guard against exactly this.

[ADVISORY] The user-storage isValid branch validates a recovery code with generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())), accepting any code at any index and never consuming or advancing the used-code counter, unlike the real single-use, index-bound validation. The backwards-compatibility test asserts login success under weaker semantics than production (a replayed code, or the wrong-index code, validates fine), so the new testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin cannot catch regressions in counter advancement for federated users, and any real federated provider modeled on this example ships replayable, index-agnostic recovery codes.

[ADVISORY] getCredentials catches the IOException from deserializing the stored recovery codes, logs, and silently omits the credential from the returned stream — the user is reported as having no recovery-codes credential while the broken blob remains stored. A corrupted stored credential makes the user vanish from every credential listing and from RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential while isConfiguredFor still returns true (it checks myUser.recoveryCodes != null directly), producing contradictory state across the credential surface and feeding the NoSuchElementException/500 path in RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean.

[ADVISORY] The local-storage fallback branch of the new createRecoveryCodesCredential (updateCredential returning false, then recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential) is exercised by no test in this diff — testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only covers the user-storage path and explicitly asserts assertUserDontHaveDBCredentials. A regression in the fallback (wrong provider id, credential stored with the wrong payload shape, double-write) ships unnoticed, and the first signal would be production users on non-supporting federated stores failing recovery-code login, since the fallback is the primary path for every federated user whose storage does not implement updateCredential for this type.

goldens.comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added recovery-codes branch of `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(...)`, the code deserializes the stored list and validates via `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`. There is no logic to consume/remove the matched code or to enforce the requested `codeNumber`/sequence (the UI/authenticator asks for a specific numbered code, implying one-time/sequential semantics). As implemented, any matching code remains valid indefinitely and can be replayed, and the new test (`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin`) would still pass, effectively certifying replayable federated recovery codes as acceptable behavior.

adjudication.rationale: The diff directly edits the `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage` test fixture (and its factory/test) to add Recovery Codes support: e.g., `supportsCredentialType` now includes `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE`, `updateCredential` stores recovery codes, and new `getCredentials`, `isConfiguredFor`, and `isValid` branches handle recovery codes. This contradicts the class-level comment stating it represents a Keycloak 4.8.3-era provider intended to remain unmodified for forward-compat testing, meaning the tests no longer exercise an unchanged “old” provider against new Keycloak behavior for this feature. That’s a specific, diff-grounded test/architecture concern rather than an immediate functional defect.

adjudication.rationale: In CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential the provider is looked up with a hard-coded id string: session.getProvider(CredentialProvider.class, "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes"). In this diff, RecoveryAuthnCodesAction removed usage/import of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID and now delegates to this helper, so the provider id is effectively duplicated (factory constant vs this literal). That’s a real, diff-grounded maintainability/robustness issue (a future rename or alternative registration id would break), though the finding’s claim that it would "silently" fall back is not supported: if getProvider returns null, the code would NPE at recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...) (no null-check).

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest), the flow performs a single recovery-code login (`enterRecoveryCodes(..., expectedCode=0, recoveryKeys)` then `clickSignInButton()`) and then only asserts success (`appPage.assertCurrent()`), without attempting a second authentication to verify that the used code was consumed (e.g., code #0 rejected or next requested code is #1). Given this PR adds federated-storage support paths for recovery codes (e.g., `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` calling `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` for user storage), a regression where post-validation updates/consumption are not routed to federated storage would not be caught by this test.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(UserModel)` which explicitly prefers federated credentials (`getFederatedCredentialsStream()`) and only then falls back to local ones (`getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...)`). The same diff also changes login/code-selection call sites to use this new method (e.g., `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` and `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`). Meanwhile, `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` attempts `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` (user storage) and otherwise creates a local credential, but it does not remove any pre-existing local credential when user storage update succeeds. From the diff alone, it is therefore possible for both a federated and a local recovery-codes credential of the same type to exist, and different code paths could observe different copies depending on whether they use `getCredential(...)` or still call `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...)`. This is a concrete, diff-grounded edge-case/consistency concern, but the diff does not prove that such dual copies will occur in practice or that any remaining consumers actually read the local copy, so it is not a strictly verifiable defect within this PR.

adjudication.rationale: In `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` the diff changes the lookup to `Optional<CredentialModel> credentialModelOpt = RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user);` but then immediately calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` without checking presence. If no recovery-codes credential exists in either federated or local storage, this will throw `NoSuchElementException` and likely result in a 500 during form rendering. The Optional-shaped API does not prevent the crash here because it is unguarded at the call site.

adjudication.rationale: In `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`, the federated-storage path builds a `UserCredentialModel` whose `challengeResponse` is `JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)` (JSON of the raw list) and calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`. If that returns false, the local-storage path instead calls `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)` and persists `credentialModel` as-is. The diff does show two independent sources of truth for the persisted payload (`generatedCodes` vs `credentialModel`), which can lead to local vs federated credential-data shape divergence if `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel`’s internal serialization ever changes. However, the diff does not prove a current functional break (it’s a forward-compat/consistency concern rather than a demonstrated defect).

adjudication.rationale: In CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential, the user-storage path serializes `generatedCodes` to JSON (`JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)`) and puts it into `new UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson)`, then calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`. The test user storage provider’s `updateCredential` branch for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` persists `input.getChallengeResponse()` directly into `CredentialModel.setCredentialData(...)`, and its `isValid` later deserializes that list and checks `key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())`, confirming plaintext-at-rest semantics for federated/user-storage backed users. This creates a clear security inconsistency/defect: recovery codes are stored verbatim in user storage via the new helper.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The user-storage contract introduced here hands providers a bare JSON array of codes in UserCredentialModel.getChallengeResponse() rather than the canonical RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel payload that RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel expects when reading the credential back. Third-party user-storage providers that follow the established OTP precedent in this same class (store challengeResponse, return the stored CredentialModel verbatim from getCredentials) will hand the authenticator a credential whose credentialData is a plain array; createFromCredentialModel in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator/RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean then fails to parse it and the code-entry page breaks. The in-repo test provider only works because BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials silently re-wraps the raw list via createFromValues, a step the CredentialHelper API does not document or enforce.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show that `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` serializes `generatedCodes` as a bare JSON array string and passes it via `new UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson)` into `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` (i.e., into user-storage). It also shows the in-repo test user-storage (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage`) stores that raw string in `CredentialModel.credentialData` and then, in `getCredentials(...)`, re-wraps it into a `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` via `createFromValues(...)` before returning it. However, the finding’s core claim—that `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel(...)` will fail to parse a credential returned “verbatim” with `credentialData` containing just the array—cannot be directly verified from this diff because the implementation/expected JSON shape of `createFromCredentialModel` isn’t shown. So this is a concrete SPI/contract risk evidenced by the changed storage shape and the test-provider workaround, but not a provable breakage solely from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The credential provider is looked up with the hardcoded string literal "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" while this same PR deletes the use of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID from RecoveryAuthnCodesAction, leaving the canonical constant unused at the new call site. If PROVIDER_ID is ever renamed, this call site silently returns null and createRecoveryCodesCredential throws an NPE instead of failing at compile time; the next change to the provider id now has to be hunted through string literals.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` which looks up the provider via a hardcoded string: `session.getProvider(CredentialProvider.class, "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes")`, and the call site in `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction` no longer uses `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID`. This is a concrete maintainability/robustness issue introduced by the change: if the provider ID ever changes, this lookup could return null and later `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)` would NPE, but the diff does not show an immediate mismatch today—so it’s not a verifiable current defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The storage provider's updateCredential blindly overwrites the stored recovery-codes credentialData with input.getChallengeResponse(), so whatever the authenticator sends when it rewrites the credential to consume the just-used code replaces the entire stored codes list. If the consume-update issued by RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator after a successful code entry carries anything other than the full remaining-codes JSON in challengeResponse, the stored credential is corrupted or wiped and every subsequent recovery-code login for that federated user fails; the new test performs exactly one recovery-code login, so a first-use code consumption bug of this shape passes CI unnoticed.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show that the backwards-compatibility federated storage provider stores recovery codes by overwriting `credentialData` with `input.getChallengeResponse()` (in `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential(...)`), while `getCredentials(...)` later assumes that `credentialData` is a JSON-serialized `List` and will fail to deserialize if it is not. The new test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` performs only a single recovery-code login and does not assert that code consumption/credential update preserves a valid remaining-codes JSON for a subsequent login, so a first-use-only scenario could pass without catching a bad “consume/update” payload shape. However, the finding’s assertion about what `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` sends on consumption is not verifiable from this diff alone, so this is best treated as a test/edge-case coverage concern rather than a confirmed defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCredential unconditionally prefers the federated credential over the locally stored one, so a federated user who already has a recovery-codes credential in the Keycloak DB (created before their storage provider gained support for the type) ends up with two credentials of the same type, and createRecoveryCodesCredential writes new setups into the storage while the stale local copy remains. After an upgrade where a storage provider starts claiming the recovery-codes type, existing users' locally stored codes are shadowed (never read, never updated, never consumed) while fresh setups fork state across two stores; used-code counters can desynchronize between the copies and the DB credential becomes an unremovable leftover from the user's perspective.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() which always returns the first federated credential of type recovery-codes if present, only falling back to local stored credentials otherwise (getFederatedCredentialsStream() ... .findFirst().or(() -> getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...).findFirst())). It also adds CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(), which first tries user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...) (writing into the user storage path when supported) and, on success, does not remove/overwrite any existing locally stored recovery-codes credential; it only creates a local one when updateCredential returns false. Together, this can leave two recovery-codes credentials (old local + new federated), with the local one becoming shadowed by getCredential() and effectively orphaned/stale after a reset when a storage provider starts supporting the type.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin covers only the single happy-path login: it never exercises a second recovery-code login, a wrong-code attempt, or the used-code consumption round-trip through the federated updateCredential path introduced by this diff. The core semantics that differentiate the storage-backed path from the local one (one-time-use enforcement and re-read of the rewritten credential) have zero coverage; a regression in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential or in the challengeResponse payload contract would ship undetected while the existing assertions stay green.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces new federated-storage behavior for recovery codes: `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` first tries `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` with a JSON `challengeResponse`, and `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential(...)` stores that JSON into `CredentialModel.credentialData` for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE`. The new test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only performs initial setup + a single successful login using one generated code; it never performs a second login to verify one-time-use/consumption, nor a wrong-code path, nor any round-trip that would force the provider’s `updateCredential` to be exercised again after code use. Given the new contract relies on the `challengeResponse` payload and federated `updateCredential` semantics, this is a concrete, diff-grounded coverage gap rather than a generic “add more tests”.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw, unhashed recovery codes (recoveryCodesJson = JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)) and hands them to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(), while the local-storage fallback path stores the hashed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel — the federated path persists plaintext recovery codes by design of this helper. Any user-storage backend following this contract (as the diff's own BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does: recoveryCodesModel.setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse()) storing the raw JSON list) holds fully usable recovery codes in plaintext in the external store (LDAP attribute, external DB), where the same codes stored locally are hashed; an attacker with read access to the user-storage backend obtains working second-factor recovery material that the local path was designed to never expose. The asymmetry contradicts the protection the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider provides.

adjudication.rationale: The new helper `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` serializes `generatedCodes` to JSON (`JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)`) and passes that string as the `challengeResponse` in a `UserCredentialModel` to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`. The diff’s own federated user-storage implementation (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential`) persists `input.getChallengeResponse()` directly into `recoveryCodesModel.setCredentialData(...)`, and later validates by deserializing that JSON list and doing direct equality checks against the presented code (`generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`). This makes the federated-storage path store fully usable recovery codes in plaintext in the external store, while the local fallback path stores a `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` via `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)` (i.e., a different representation with different protections). The diff therefore introduces/solidifies a security-relevant asymmetry where read-access to the user-storage backend yields working 2FA recovery material.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new recovery-codes branch of isValid() validates with generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())), which accepts any of the user's codes regardless of which code number the login flow requested and never consumes or invalidates a used code — deviating from the position-bound, one-time semantics of the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider this PR claims compatibility with. Because this provider is the reference implementation of the new user-storage recovery-codes SPI contract introduced by this PR, the demonstrated contract is 'set-membership check on plaintext codes with no position binding and no single-use enforcement': a code entered for position 7 is accepted when code 3 was requested, and a compromised or observed code remains valid forever. The compatibility test suite then validates and blesses weaker validation semantics than production recovery-code behavior.

adjudication.rationale: In BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(), the new recovery-codes branch deserializes the stored List and validates with `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`, which is a pure set-membership check. The diff shows no binding to the UI-requested code number (see RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean using `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get().getNumber()` to prompt a specific index) and no consumption/invalidation of a used code in this provider (isValid only reads and compares; it never updates storedRecoveryKeys/recoveryCodes). As a result, any valid code can satisfy any prompt and codes remain reusable, which weakens expected one-time/position semantics and makes the added compatibility test less strict.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCredential() resolves the federated credential first and only falls back to the locally stored credential via .or(), so when a user has both, the federated copy silently shadows the local one for both rendering (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean) and validation (RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator). A user whose credential was previously written to local storage (hashed, position-bound, single-use) and who is later federated with a storage that claims support for the type gets the federated plaintext, replayable copy used for every validation; the better-protected local credential is unreachable through this lookup, and the write path in createRecoveryCodesCredential reinforces the same preference, leaving the stale local copy permanently orphaned.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(UserModel)` which explicitly prefers federated credentials (`getFederatedCredentialsStream()...findFirst()`) and only falls back to local credentials via `.or(() -> getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...)...)`. This new lookup is then used for both rendering (`RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`) and validation (`RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`), replacing the prior local-only lookup. As a result, when both a federated and local recovery-codes credential exist, the federated one will silently shadow the local one and the local copy becomes effectively unreachable through these code paths. The write path `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` similarly tries `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` first (which targets user storage) and only creates a local credential if that returns false, reinforcing the preference and leaving an existing local credential potentially orphaned.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The constructor calls credentialModelOpt.get() on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without an isPresent check, throwing NoSuchElementException when the user has no recovery-codes credential in either federated or local storage. If the recovery-codes authenticator renders the challenge for a user with no resolvable credential (e.g., storage reports the type as configured but getCredentials() returns an empty stream, or a storage error path leaves neither location populated), the freemarker render fails with NoSuchElementException and the user gets a server error page instead of a graceful authentication failure or redirect.

adjudication.rationale: In `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` the constructor now does `Optional<CredentialModel> credentialModelOpt = RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user);` and then immediately calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` with no presence check. Since `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` can return `Optional.empty()` (no federated and no stored credential found), this will throw `NoSuchElementException` during page rendering, leading to a server error rather than graceful handling if the bean is instantiated for a user without a resolvable recovery-codes credential.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new fallback branch in createRecoveryCodesCredential (updateCredential returning false -> recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential locally) is never exercised by the only test added in this diff, which exclusively covers the storage-hit path. The diff's test (testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin) uses BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage whose updateCredential always returns true for recovery codes, so the else-branch that persists locally is unverified by any test in this diff; a regression there (e.g., wrong credentialModel passed to createCredential) would only surface for non-federated users, outside this test. Checked test files in the diff: testsuite/integration-arquillian/tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/federation/storage/BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.java — it contains no case where updateCredential returns false.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new two-path behavior in CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(): it first calls user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...), and only if that returns false does it fall back to recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel). The only added test (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest#testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin) uses BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage, whose updateCredential(...) branch for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE explicitly ends with `return true;`, so the fallback `else` branch cannot be exercised by this test. Therefore the finding that the local-storage fallback path is unverified by tests in this diff is correct and specific to the added logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new .or() fallback in getCredential (federated stream empty -> look in getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream) is not triggered by the test added in this diff, because the federated storage always returns the credential first. If the lookup ordering or the or() supplier itself regresses (e.g., the wrong type filter in the stored-credentials stream), the diff's only new test still passes because it never reaches the fallback; a federated-less user's recovery-code lookup breakage would be invisible to this diff's verification. Checked BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.java — the user 'otp1' is federated with recovery codes present, so findFirst() always succeeds and or() is dead in the test.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(UserModel) which first searches user.credentialManager().getFederatedCredentialsStream() and only falls back via Optional.or(...) to getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...). The only new test (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest#testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin) sets up recovery codes in the federated user storage (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential stores myUser.recoveryCodes and returns true), and even asserts the user has recovery keys in user storage. Therefore getFederatedCredentialsStream().findFirst() will succeed and the .or(...) fallback path is not exercised by this new test, so regressions in the fallback lookup would not be caught by this PR’s added verification.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new recovery-codes branch of isValid() has three failure returns (storedRecoveryKeys == null, IOException on deserialization, no matching key) and the diff's test never submits an incorrect or missing credential, so none of these branches is exercised. The fixture's negative path is unverified: if the anyMatch comparison or the null/deserialization guards were wrong (e.g., accepting any input), testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin would still pass because it only enters the correct code from the page; the suite gives no signal that wrong codes are actually rejected for storage-backed users. Checked BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.java — enterRecoveryCodes only enters generatedRecoveryAuthnCodes.get(requestedCode), never a wrong value.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new recovery-codes validation path in `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(...)` with multiple failure/negative outcomes (`storedRecoveryKeys == null` -> false, JSON deserialization `IOException` -> false, and `anyMatch(...)` naturally returning false when no code matches). The newly added test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin()` only performs a successful login by submitting `generatedRecoveryAuthnCodes.get(requestedCode)` via `enterRecoveryCodes(...)`, and does not attempt an incorrect code or missing credential scenario. Therefore, the new negative/guard branches in the recovery-codes validation logic are not exercised by the tests introduced/modified in this diff, leaving a specific, diff-grounded gap in coverage for storage-backed recovery codes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin verifies only a single successful use of recovery code 0 and contains no assertion that the used code is invalidated (re-login rejects it or the next login demands code 1), so non-single-use behavior of storage-backed recovery codes passes the suite undetected. The new BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid branch compares the input with generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(...) and never consumes the used code; if code consumption does not round-trip through the federated storage, a federated user can replay the same recovery code forever, and this test — the only one in the diff covering the storage-backed login — stays green because it stops after the first successful login and never logs in again.

adjudication.rationale: The new test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` performs only one successful recovery-code login (it enters the requested code and asserts `appPage.assertCurrent()`), then logs out, and never attempts a second login to verify single-use semantics (e.g., that the same code is rejected or that the next prompt requests code #1). Separately, the added `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid` branch for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` only checks `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))` and does not itself remove/consume the used code; whether consumption happens elsewhere isn’t shown in this diff. Therefore the finding is a concrete, diff-grounded gap in coverage for the new federated-storage path, but a definitive replay bug cannot be proven from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCredentials() swallows the IOException from deserializing the stored recovery codes and silently returns the stream without that credential, while the parallel isValid() path in the same class treats the same corruption as a failed validation, so the two read paths disagree on the same corrupted state. If the serialized credentialData format drifts (exactly the scenario a backwards-compatibility fixture exists to catch), getCredentials silently drops the credential — getCredential() in RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils then finds nothing and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean's credentialModelOpt.get() throws NoSuchElementException — and the log.error (which omits the exception itself) is the only trace, making fixture failures hard to diagnose; the divergence from isValid's return-false handling means a corrupted credential is 'absent' for listing but 'invalid' for login.

adjudication.rationale: In BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials(), the new recovery-codes branch catches IOException from JsonSerialization.readValue(...) and only logs a generic message (no exception) before continuing, which means the recovery-codes credential is silently omitted from the returned Stream. In the same class, isValid() handles the same deserialization failure by returning false. This creates an inconsistent view of corrupted/changed credentialData: listing/lookup sees “no credential”, while validation sees “invalid credential”. That omission can propagate: RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) looks at federated credentials first, and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean then calls credentialModelOpt.get() without a presence check, so a dropped credential can trigger a NoSuchElementException with little diagnostic information.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential switches the write path to user-storage-first without any cleanup or migration of a pre-existing locally-stored recovery-codes credential, so re-running the setup action for a federated user creates a second copy of the codes in the user storage while the old DB copy stays behind. For a federated user who already has recovery codes in the local DB (the only place the pre-change code wrote them — the old authenticator read getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream exclusively and it worked, proving old writes were local), re-running CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES after upgrade writes a new copy into the user storage; RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential reads federated-first, so the DB copy is permanently shadowed yet remains a live, valid credential set that no path in this diff ever removes — two divergent code sets in two stores, and the local one resurfaces if the storage-side copy is ever deleted.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential() which attempts user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...) first and, if that returns true, never cleans up any existing locally-stored recovery-codes credential (it only logs; it does not call any remove on stored credentials). Previously, RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.processAction() always wrote via recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...), i.e., to local storage. After this change, a federated user with an existing local RecoveryAuthnCodes credential who now has a user storage that supports updateCredential for that type can end up with two credentials (one in user storage and the old one still in local DB). RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() is changed to prefer federated credentials first and only then fall back to local, so the old DB credential becomes shadowed but remains present and could be used again if the federated one is removed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The write path (user-storage-first here) and the read path (federated-first in RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential) both change in one release with no transition guard, creating a rolling-deploy skew where an old-version pod's authenticator still reads only getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream. In a mixed-version cluster, a user of a storage provider that supports the recovery-codes type sets up codes on a new-version pod (stored only in user storage); when the login attempt lands on an old-version pod, isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid finds no stored credential and rejects the user with INVALID_CREDENTIALS until every pod is upgraded. Today only the testsuite BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage declares support, so production impact is nil until third-party providers adopt the type, but the pattern has no expand/contract transition.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the write path for recovery codes to prefer user storage by calling `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` with a JSON payload (in `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential`), only falling back to local storage if that returns false. At the same time, new read sites are updated to look in both federated and local storage via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(...)`, but an older (pre-diff) node would still read only `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE)` (as shown by the removed code in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`). In a mixed-version/rolling upgrade, a new node can store recovery codes only in user storage, and an old node will not find them in local storage and will reject login, so the finding’s rolling-deploy skew is consistent with what this diff changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCredentials silently drops the recovery-codes credential on a JSON deserialization failure (log.error only, model not added), so the credential disappears from the federated stream without any error surfaced to the caller. When credentialData cannot be parsed, getCredential falls through to the local store (also empty), RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean's credentialModelOpt.get() throws NoSuchElementException, and the user gets a 500-style error on the login page instead of a meaningful message — the data corruption is masked as a missing credential with only a server-side log line.

adjudication.rationale: In BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials(), recovery-codes are deserialized from JSON and on IOException the code only logs (log.error) and does not add any CredentialModel to the returned stream, effectively making the federated recovery-codes credential “disappear” to callers. RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) then won’t find a federated credential and may return Optional.empty() if local storage also lacks it. RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean now calls RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) and immediately does credentialModelOpt.get() with no presence check, which will throw NoSuchElementException and can surface as a 500-style error during login rather than a controlled/meaningful error, matching the finding’s described failure mode.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean constructor calls credentialModelOpt.get() on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user), throwing NoSuchElementException (rendered as a raw 500) whenever no recovery-codes credential is found in either store. The new federated-first lookup introduces a reachable empty case the old code did not have: for a federated user whose storage reports the credential as configured (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isConfiguredFor returns true whenever myUser.recoveryCodes != null) but whose getCredentials drops the credential because JSON deserialization failed (the IOException catch at lines ~238-240 of the storage swallows it and returns the credential list without it), getCredential finds nothing in the federated stream and nothing locally, and the bean constructor throws NoSuchElementException mid-login-flow, producing a 500 error page instead of a graceful flow failure.

adjudication.rationale: In `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` the constructor now does `Optional<CredentialModel> credentialModelOpt = RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user);` and then immediately calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` with no presence check. From the diff, `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` can legitimately return `Optional.empty()` when neither a federated credential nor a local stored credential of type `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` exists. Additionally, the diff introduces a concrete way for this to happen even when the user-storage claims the credential is configured: `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isConfiguredFor(...)` returns true when `myUser.recoveryCodes != null`, but `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials(...)` will drop the recovery-codes credential on JSON deserialization failure (it catches `IOException`, logs, and does not add the credential to the returned stream). In that case, `getCredential()` finds nothing and the bean will throw `NoSuchElementException`, leading to a server error during rendering/flow.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] When user.credentialManager().updateCredential() returns false, the credential is silently re-created in the local Keycloak DB with no log line on the else branch — the only logged path is the successful user-storage write. Operators and admins auditing where recovery codes live get zero trace of the fallback: a deployment that expects codes persisted in the federated user store silently ends up with them only in the Keycloak DB, and debugging 'where did the codes go' after a storage-provider change has no log to start from.

adjudication.rationale: In `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`, the code logs only when `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(recoveryCodesCredential)` returns true (`logger.debugf("Created RecoveryCodes credential ... in the user storage")`). When it returns false, it falls back to `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel);` with no corresponding log line. This matches the finding: the fallback to local Keycloak storage is silent/undiscoverable from logs, which is an operational/auditing concern rather than a correctness defect shown by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The credential provider is looked up with the hardcoded string literal "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" while the diff removes the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID import, so a future rename of the provider id compiles cleanly but getProvider returns null. On the local-fallback path (updateCredential returning false), recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential would throw a NullPointerException during the required-action request, surfacing as a 500 at the exact moment a user is setting up their recovery codes; the removed constant was the compile-time guard against exactly this.

adjudication.rationale: In `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`, the provider is obtained via a hardcoded literal: `session.getProvider(CredentialProvider.class, "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes")`. The diff also removes the previous use/import of `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID` in `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction` and routes creation through this helper. There is no null-check before `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)`, so if the string ever drifts from the actual provider id (e.g., future rename) the code would compile but fail at runtime. This is a concrete diff-grounded maintainability/robustness issue, but not a verifiable defect in current behavior from the diff alone because we cannot confirm the id is wrong or that `getProvider(...)` can be null in the intended runtime configuration.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The user-storage isValid branch validates a recovery code with generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())), accepting any code at any index and never consuming or advancing the used-code counter, unlike the real single-use, index-bound validation. The backwards-compatibility test asserts login success under weaker semantics than production (a replayed code, or the wrong-index code, validates fine), so the new testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin cannot catch regressions in counter advancement for federated users, and any real federated provider modeled on this example ships replayable, index-agnostic recovery codes.

adjudication.rationale: In BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(), the newly added recovery-codes branch deserializes the stored JSON list and validates with `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`, without checking the requested code number/index and without mutating stored state to consume/advance a used-code counter. Given the surrounding recovery-codes flow asks for a specific numbered code (see EnterRecoveryAuthnCodePage usage and RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.getNextRecoveryAuthnCode()), this makes recovery codes replayable and index-agnostic for this user-storage implementation, and the added test would pass under these weaker semantics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCredentials catches the IOException from deserializing the stored recovery codes, logs, and silently omits the credential from the returned stream — the user is reported as having no recovery-codes credential while the broken blob remains stored. A corrupted stored credential makes the user vanish from every credential listing and from RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential while isConfiguredFor still returns true (it checks myUser.recoveryCodes != null directly), producing contradictory state across the credential surface and feeding the NoSuchElementException/500 path in RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage#getCredentials(...)` which attempts to deserialize `myUser.recoveryCodes.getCredentialData()` and, on `IOException`, logs an error and returns a stream without the recovery-codes credential (it is simply not added to `credentialModels`). Meanwhile `isConfiguredFor(...)` was updated to return `true` for recovery codes solely based on `myUser.recoveryCodes != null`, so a corrupted/undecodable blob yields contradictory state: configured=true but the credential never appears in credential listings/streams. Since `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` relies on credential streams, it will also miss the credential in that case, and callers like `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` do `credentialModelOpt.get()` without checking presence, enabling a `NoSuchElementException`/500 path when this inconsistency occurs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The local-storage fallback branch of the new createRecoveryCodesCredential (updateCredential returning false, then recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential) is exercised by no test in this diff — testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only covers the user-storage path and explicitly asserts assertUserDontHaveDBCredentials. A regression in the fallback (wrong provider id, credential stored with the wrong payload shape, double-write) ships unnoticed, and the first signal would be production users on non-supporting federated stores failing recovery-code login, since the fallback is the primary path for every federated user whose storage does not implement updateCredential for this type.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds nontrivial branching logic in `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`: it first calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` and only if that returns false does it fall back to `session.getProvider(CredentialProvider.class, "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes").createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)`. The new test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` uses the modified `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage` which explicitly supports `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` and returns `true` from `updateCredential(...)` for that type, and the test asserts `assertUserDontHaveDBCredentials()`, so it exercises only the user-storage branch and not the local-storage fallback branch. No other added test in this diff targets the fallback path.
